terms.grammar: adjective, comparative in form; genitive interiōris
evidence: Cic. Sest. 10: in interiōre aedium parte (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: A comparative with no positive (superlative intimus, innermost): the inner part of a house, the inland peoples (Cic. Imp. Pomp. 22), the inside of anything; as a neuter plural noun, interiōra, the inside (Vulg. Jon. 1.5). The i is a vowel. A state’s internal affairs and wars are intestīnus or domesticus (Cic. Cat. 2.28; see civil, domestic).
Post-Augustan (Lewis & Short); in Tacitus mostly of a state’s own affairs and quarrels (discordiae, Ann. 2.26).

phrases.latin: et Jōnās dēscendit ad interiōra nāvis, et dormiēbat sopōre gravī
phrases.english: and Jonah went down into the inside of the ship and lay fast asleep

phrases.latin: nōn semper ea sunt quae videntur; dēcipit frōns prīma multōs; rāra mēns intellegit quod interiōre condidit cūra angulō
phrases.english: things are not always what they seem; first appearances deceive many; few minds see what care has hidden in an inner corner

sources: Lewis & Short: interior · Lewis & Short: internus · Lewis & Short: intestinus
Quotations from the Latinitas loci collections (loci-vulgata, loci-phaedrus), checked against the editions named there. Cicero, Vergil and Seneca as Lewis & Short quotes them.
